Problem 85. Change and continuity in a settlement: case 5
History studies both change and continuity. Comparing two snapshots is a systematic way to separate what persisted from what appeared or disappeared.
Period 1 features: footpath, market, wall, well, wooden bridge. Period 2 features: market, park, road, stone bridge, well.

A continuity is a feature present in both periods. A disappearance is present only in Period 1. An appearance is present only in Period 2. A replacement can be described when two differently named features serve the same stated role.
Identify the continuities, disappearances, and appearances. Which conclusions are direct set comparisons rather than interpretations?

1. Intersection gives continuities: ['market', 'well']. 2. Period1−Period2 gives disappearances: ['footpath', 'wall', 'wooden bridge']. 3. Period2−Period1 gives appearances: ['park', 'road', 'stone bridge']. 4. Only role-based replacement would require extra information; the set comparisons are direct.
Change is not the opposite of continuity; both can occur in the same community at the same time.
Set operations: intersection for continuity, set difference for appearance/disappearance.
Problem 86. Reading an archaeological sequence: case 1
Archaeological layers provide relative chronological information. Dates from objects add constraints but do not automatically make every date exact.

An undisturbed archaeological site has four layers from top to bottom: A, B, C, D. In an undisturbed sequence, lower layers were deposited earlier. D contains an object dated 1300, C contains one dated 1450, and B contains one dated 1600.

In an undisturbed sequence, a lower layer is older than a layer above it. A securely dated object provides a constraint on the layer that contains it, but one object does not date every other object exactly.
Which is older, Layer C or Layer B? Can the exact year of deposition of Layer A be deduced?

1. C lies below B, so C is older than B by the stratigraphic rule. 2. No exact dated object or deposition year is given for A. 3. Therefore only relative ordering, not an exact year for A, is justified.
Layer C is older than Layer B. The exact deposition year of Layer A cannot be deduced.
Relative dating and absolute dating answer different questions and should not be confused.
Partial order from vertical position plus numeric constraints from dated objects.

Problem 91. Applying a rule with an exception: Owen
Rules often have conditions and exceptions. Logical reading prevents us from applying a general rule when an overriding exception is active.

Owen is 10 years old. A library rule says: a child may enter the archive room if age ≥ 11 AND an adult permit is present. Exception: during an evacuation drill, nobody may enter. Permit present: yes. Evacuation drill: no.
Check exceptions first if they override the general rule. Otherwise every condition joined by AND must be true.
May Owen enter the archive room under these facts? Show which conditions succeed or fail.
1. Age test: 10≥11 is False. 2. Permit test is True. 3. Because the general rule uses AND, both tests must pass. 4. Therefore entry is not allowed.
The order of reasoning matters when exceptions override ordinary rules.
Boolean rule with priority: exception predicate first, then conjunction of eligibility conditions.
